idiom_name: ASP.NET Core output caching middleware (AddOutputCache / CacheOutput / [OutputCache])
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core's output caching middleware is the framework's page cache: builder.Services.AddOutputCache(...) with named policies (Expire, SetVaryByHeader, VaryByQueryKeys), app.UseOutputCache() and per-endpoint .CacheOutput() or [OutputCache] store the finished response on the server - keyed by method, path and query - so the action, its data access and its view never run on a hit. The defaults are conservative and worth knowing: only GET/HEAD 200 responses are cached, responses that set cookies are not cached, responses to authenticated requests are not cached unless a policy overrides it, and entries are invalidated by expiry or programmatically through IOutputCacheStore.EvictByTagAsync. It replaces the older header-driven Response Caching Middleware, which replayed HTTP freshness metadata only, could be defeated by the client's own request headers and offered neither programmatic invalidation nor revalidation.
pitfalls: Middleware order is semantic: UseOutputCache must run after UseRouting, UseCors and UseAuthentication/UseAuthorization, or a response cached for one caller can be replayed to another.

Overriding the default policy to cache authenticated or cookie-setting responses reintroduces the per-user leak the defaults were designed to prevent: vary on the authorisation-relevant key or leave those endpoints uncached.
Cache entries survive deploys in a distributed store; without a purge or tag eviction on release, users keep seeing the previous build's pages until the expiry lapses.

variants.name: ASP.NET Core output caching middleware (.NET 7+)
Response Caching Middleware with [ResponseCache] attributes
variants.implementation_notes: Header-driven variant: [ResponseCache] (or ResponseCacheAttribute conventions) writes the HTTP freshness metadata and app.UseResponseCaching() lets the middleware replay a stored response when the request's own Cache-Control allows it. It is deliberately standards-shaped but weak on the server side - the client can defeat it (browsers send max-age=0 on reload), storage is memory-only, and there is no programmatic eviction and no revalidation - so it fits public GET/HEAD endpoints that should be cacheable by proxies and CDNs rather than UI pages, which Microsoft's own guidance points at output caching instead. Choose it when the real cache lives in front of the app and you only need the origin to state the contract correctly.
pitfalls: Because caching is negotiated through request headers, a client sending Cache-Control: no-cache (every browser on reload) gets a full render - do not expect an origin-side speed-up from this variant.
There is no eviction API: invalidation means waiting out Duration, changing the URL, or purging the intermediary that actually stored the response.
